summary: Wilde, aged twenty-three, complained to Harold Boulton that he had not written, that music made him forget everybody else, and that he believed Boulton liked another young man - emphasised - much better than himself.

sources.quote: My dear Harold, I really never expected to hear from you again. I wish music was not such a siren to you as to make you forget everybody else. Will you come and see me tonight at nine o'clock or any time when you can escape from 'Sir John' - whom by the bye I believe you like _much better_ than yours truly … I have some men dining tonight with me - not very intellectual - but you will find Vaughan Hughes amongst them.
sources.context: Wilde to Harold Boulton, [? April 1878], Magdalen College (MS Yale) - quoted whole; the ellipsis marks where the signature falls, mid-letter, before the postscript. 'much better' is underlined in the original. The editors identify 'Sir John' as most probably Sir John Alexander Hanham, ninth Baronet, a Magdalen undergraduate of 1875-8. Wilde was twenty-three; Boulton was eighteen or nineteen and about to go up to Balliol.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde jealous of a young man's preference for someone else, and emphasising it.

manuscript.repository: Yale University Library, New Haven, Connecticut
